mainKeyword: solar generator to run a refrigerator
guideTitle: Best Solar Generators to Run a Refrigerator (2026)
metaTitle: Best Solar Generators to Run a Refrigerator
metaDescription: Six solar generators that can keep a refrigerator cold on sunshine alone, with panel sizing math for a daily fridge load of about one and a half kilowatt-hours.
expertTake: The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 with two 200W panels is the best pick for running a refrigerator on solar alone, because 400W of panels and a 2,042Wh tank roughly match a typical fridge's daily energy. The UDPOWER S1200 is the value route if your refrigerator is modern and efficient. Skip kits with 100W of panels or less if you hope to go off-grid, since they only stretch battery time.
introParagraphs: Running a refrigerator from battery for an evening is easy. Running it from the sun, day after day, is a sizing problem with three parts: the daily energy the fridge uses, the panel power available to harvest it, and a battery big enough to carry the compressor through the night.

This guide treats each product as a small off-grid system. For each we estimate hours of battery runtime and what the included or recommended panels can contribute on a decent day, so you can see which setups truly sustain a refrigerator and which only delay the inevitable.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 with 2x200W Solar Panels
products.description:
This kit comes closest to solving the whole equation in one box. Four hundred watts of panels give roughly 1,200Wh on a decent day after real-world losses, and a modern refrigerator uses about 1,000 to 1,500Wh a day, so the sun can nearly cover the load while the 2,042Wh battery covers the nights and cloudy gaps.

The inverter is 2,200W, so compressor startup is a non-event, and the listing's 39.5 pound weight makes it manageable for one person. It also does a 66 minute recharge to 80 percent from the wall, which helps if a long gray spell forces a top-up from the grid.

The weakness is winter: a 400W array can fall below 500Wh on a short overcast day, so if you rely on it in December, add panels or a generator. Tilt the panels toward the sun, keep them clear of snow and shade, and rinse them when they get dirty. If your refrigerator is in a garage in a hot climate, expect the compressor to run longer and budget an extra 20 percent.
products.bestFor: People who want a refrigerator to run on sun with minimal fuss.
pros: 400W panel kit nearly matches a fridge's daily need
Quick recharge from the wall in a gray spell
cons: Short winter days leave a deficit
Premium cost for just a refrigerator

products.name: ABOK Ark3600 3,840Wh with 3x200W Solar Panels
products.description:
With 600W of panels and a 3,840Wh tank, the Ark3600 is the one that keeps a refrigerator and a chest freezer going on sun, with room for lights and a router. On a decent day 600W of panels produce around 1,900Wh, which covers a fridge and a freezer together, and the big tank rides out the bad days that smaller batteries cannot.

It is overkill for a refrigerator alone, but the extra capacity pays when the load grows: a sump pump, a few lights and a laptop all fit without recalculating. Expansion packs take it to 11,520Wh, and the combined AC and solar input lets you refill quickly from either source.

Three panels demand real ground area and anchoring. Keep the vents clear, check the panel cables each season and store the unit half charged if the refrigerator is only a seasonal worry. Because the kit's three panels are rigid, a ground rack or pole mount saves you from re-aiming them by hand every morning.
products.bestFor: Households running a refrigerator plus a freezer and a few extras on solar.
pros: 600W of panels refill about 1,900Wh a day
Fast combined AC and solar charging
cons: Three panels need serious ground space

products.name: Anker SOLIX S2000 Solar Generator, 2,010Wh 1,500W
products.description:
A refrigerator is a steady, low-power load, which is exactly where the S2000's 6W idle draw helps. Anker claims up to 35 hours of fridge backup from the 2,010Wh pack, which implies an average draw near 57W and shows how much runtime depends on inverter overhead rather than raw capacity.

There are no panels in this listing, so the solar side is your choice. A 200W folding panel yields about 600Wh a day, enough to cover roughly 40 percent of a refrigerator's day, and a pair gets you to self-sufficiency in good weather. The ten-thousand-cycle LFP cells make it the longest-lived pack here by a wide margin.

Think of it as the efficient battery to which you add the panels that suit your yard. Wipe the vents, keep the case dry and avoid freezing temperatures during charging. Because the cells are quoted at 10,000 cycles, the battery is unlikely to be the part that wears out first.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the most refrigerator hours per watt-hour and will choose their own panels.
pros: 10,000-cycle LFP cells for a very long life
cons: Newer model with little track record

products.name: Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 with 200W Solar Panel
products.description:
Here is the entry point for a refrigerator on solar, with an honest caveat. A 200W panel yields roughly 600Wh on a good day, a bit under half of what a typical refrigerator needs in 24 hours, so the 1,024Wh battery bridges the rest. That means about a day and a half of cold food without grid help, and longer if the sun is generous.

The 1,500W inverter and 3,000W surge are comfortable for the compressor, and the unit is light enough to stash in a closet. Against the Jackery 2000 v2 it has half the panel power and half the tank, which is why it is a stretch rather than a solution for multi-day outages.

Use it for short outages or a camper trailer fridge, and add a second 200W panel if you want to go further. Keep it half charged in storage and recharge from the wall after any long run. The 10ms switchover claimed on the listing means it can sit between the wall and the refrigerator and take over during an outage without a reset.
products.bestFor: Small households or campers with a modern efficient refrigerator.
pros: 200W panel offsets about 40 percent of a fridge day
cons: One panel cannot sustain a fridge alone
About a day and a half of runtime without help
Little margin if the fridge is old

products.name: UDPOWER S1200 with 120W Solar Panel, 1,190Wh
products.description:
Where the Jackery kit is premium, the S1200 is the thrifty version of the same idea. A 120W panel adds about 380Wh on a good day and the 1,190Wh pack carries a modern refrigerator for roughly 15 hours on its own, so a long cloudy stretch will outpace it.

The inverter is rated 1,200W with an 1,800W peak, which clears most refrigerators but is tight on large ones. The listing notes a sub-0.01 second switchover and says the panel ships separately from the station.

Plan to add panels if you want it to carry you for days. Check the connector type on any extra panel against the station's solar input before you order, and store it at moderate charge. A watt meter on the refrigerator for a full day tells you quickly whether this unit is enough or a bigger one is needed.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers with a small, efficient refrigerator.
pros: Panel included for solar topping up
cons: 120W panel only offsets a fraction of daily use
1,200W rating is tight for large fridges

products.name: Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus Power Station, 3,584Wh
products.description:
This is the pick when your worst-case plan is a stormy week with little sun. A 3,584Wh tank carries a modern refrigerator for around two days by itself, and extra battery packs take that to many days. It is the largest runtime in the guide, with no panels attached, so the solar side is whatever you bolt on.

The listing mentions a plug-and-play route into a house through a manual transfer switch, so the refrigerator, freezer and a few lights can all hang from one box. Against the Anker S2000 it has 1,574Wh more energy and a stronger inverter but a higher idle draw.

Because there is no included array, treat it as a large battery you recharge from the grid or a generator, with panels as a bonus. Store it at moderate charge, check the vents each season and run it on a real load now and then. Pairing it with two 400W panels turns it from a standby tank into a genuine off-grid fridge power plant.
products.bestFor: Storm-prone homes that need days of refrigeration without relying on sun.
pros: 3,584Wh runs a fridge for about two days
cons: Heavy and expensive for a refrigerator alone
Higher idle draw than the S2000

buyingCriteria.explanation: A modern 18 cubic foot refrigerator uses roughly 1,000 to 1,500Wh a day, an older or crowded one 2,000Wh or more. Check the yellow EnergyGuide label for kilowatt-hours per year and divide by 365. That number, not the running watts, sizes your solar. A fridge that sits in a hot kitchen or is packed with warm groceries runs longer cycles and uses more.

Daily harvest is panel watts times 4 to 5 sun hours times 0.7 for real-world losses. A 200W panel yields about 600Wh and the Jackery 2000 v2's 400W kit about 1,200Wh. To fully offset a 1,400Wh day you need around 450 to 500W.

The refrigerator keeps running after sunset, so the battery must carry about 60 percent of the daily load. A 1,024Wh Jackery 1000 v2 or 1,190Wh UDPOWER covers a night with little margin, while the Anker S2000's 2,010Wh and the ABOK's 3,840Wh ride out a cloudy day too.

December sun hours can drop to 2 or 3, cutting a 400W array's output below 600Wh. If you need year-round self-sufficiency, plan for twice the panels or a backup source. The ABOK's 600W kit holds up better than the 120W UDPOWER set.

The station must accept the panels' voltage and current, and the connector must match. The Anker lists no panels, so verify input range before buying a third-party panel. A mismatch can mean a station that never reaches full solar charge.

An inverter that idles at 15W burns 360Wh a day, a quarter of a refrigerator's load. The Anker S2000 lists 6W. Run short, thick panel cables and keep the inverter off when the fridge is not on the unit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Sun-powered sustainability
howWeEvaluated.description: We estimated daily harvest from each kit's panels with a 4.5 sun hour and 0.7 loss assumption. The Jackery 2000 v2 kit lands near 1,260Wh and the ABOK near 1,890Wh, while the UDPOWER and Jackery 1000 v2 sit below half a day's need.

howWeEvaluated.title: Overnight and cloudy-day reserve
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether the battery carries a refrigerator through the night plus a poor day. The HomePower 3600 Plus and ABOK gave the longest reserve, the 1,024Wh class the shortest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Compressor start
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared each inverter to typical compressor startup. All units here clear it, but the 1,200W UDPOWER has the least margin.

howWeEvaluated.title: Efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored low idle draw and efficient charging, which is why the Anker S2000 stood out. Real-world savings depend on how the inverter is used.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We drew on the spec sheets and owner feedback patterns for weight, expandability and support. We make no claim of personal use.

howToChoose.subheading: By How Self-Sufficient You Want to Be

cards.label: Bigger battery
cards.text: The HomePower 3600 Plus and ABOK Ark3600 store days of fridge energy, so cloudy stretches do not hurt. You pay for tank weight and the grid recharges it when the sun fails.

cards.label: Bigger array
cards.text: The Jackery 2000 v2 kit and ABOK kit lean on harvest, so the battery refills daily. Better if you stay put and have sun.

howToChoose.note: A battery of at least one full day plus 400W of panels is the practical middle.

rows: Big tank, don't care about idle

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a large battery and extra panel capacity, since December harvest can fall to a third of summer's. Do not charge lithium below freezing, so keep the station indoors.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ABOK Ark3600 with 600W of panels and 3,840Wh holds up best. The 120W UDPOWER kit will lose ground quickly.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want the refrigerator to run through weeks of outage or you live where winters are dark. The ABOK Ark3600 kit or HomePower 3600 Plus pays for itself.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Outages are rare and short. The Jackery 1000 v2 or UDPOWER S1200 covers a day or two.

faq.q: How many solar panels do I need to run a refrigerator?
faq.a: About 400 to 500W of real panels for a modern fridge. Multiply panel watts by 4.5 sun hours and 0.7 to estimate daily watt-hours, then compare to 1,000 to 1,500Wh.

faq.q: Can a refrigerator run on a single 200W panel?
faq.a: Only partly. A 200W panel yields about 600Wh a day, so the battery covers the rest. Add a second panel to move closer to self-sufficiency.

faq.q: Which is the best value to run a fridge on solar?
faq.a: The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 kit gives the right panel and battery balance, while the UDPOWER S1200 is the budget compromise. Value depends on how long you want to run without grid power. Either way, size the battery to carry a full night and one bad day.

faq.q: Does a bigger inverter help with solar?
faq.a: No. The inverter only needs to start the compressor and carry other loads. Solar performance depends on panel watts and input limits.

Not if the battery is big enough. A 2,000Wh battery carries a refrigerator through a poor day. Longer gray spells need grid recharging or more panels. Keep the freezer closed and the refrigerator door shut as much as possible during a cloudy stretch.

faq.q: Is it safe to leave the fridge on the battery all the time?
faq.a: Pass-through works but adds heat and cell wear. For permanent setups, a station built for it or a periodic cycle is better.
